section.title: The Waters of Marah
section.sectionRationale: Only three days after singing at the sea, Israel grumbles over bitter water. This short scene introduces the wilderness pattern that will repeat again and again: need, complaint, God's provision, and a test of whether Israel will trust and obey.
section.thesis: Three days into the wilderness with no water, then bitter water they cannot drink, Israel grumbles against Moses; the LORD sweetens the water through a log He shows Moses, tests His people there, and reveals Himself as the LORD who heals, before leading them to abundant rest at Elim.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the bitter water at Marah, God's provision, and His covenant test and promise; and the rest and abundance found afterward at Elim.

verses.text: Then Moses led Israel from the Red Sea, and they went out into the Desert of Shur. For three days they walked in the desert without finding water.
And when they came to {{marah|Marah}}, they could not drink the water there because it was bitter. (That is why it was named Marah.)
So the people grumbled against Moses, saying, “What are we to drink?”

And Moses cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log. And when he cast it into the waters, they were sweetened. 
There the LORD made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there He tested them,

saying, “If you will listen carefully to the voice of the LORD your God, and do what is right in His eyes, and pay attention to His commands, and keep all His statutes, then I will not bring on you any of the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians. For I am the LORD who {{heals|heals}} you.”
Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the waters.

marah.gloss: Bitter. The place is named for the taste of its water, but the word also echoes Israel's bitterness of spirit in grumbling so soon after singing at the sea, only three days before.

heals.gloss: To heal, to make whole. The LORD names Himself here Yahweh Rapha, the LORD who heals, tying His covenant faithfulness directly to bodily wholeness and, by implication, to every kind of restoration His people need.

basic.context: Just three days after singing God's praises at the sea, Israel hits its first real test: no water, then bitter water they cannot drink. They complain to Moses, and God sweetens the water through a simple log, then uses the moment to test them and reveal Himself as their healer.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real event in Israel's early wilderness wandering. It is not a magical formula about logs healing water, but a lesson about how quickly people who have seen great grace can grumble under small pressure, and about God's pattern of providing exactly what His people need while testing whether they will trust Him.
basic.originalLanguages: The place is named marah, bitter, for its undrinkable water, a fitting picture of Israel's own bitter complaint so soon after their song of praise. God then reveals Himself as the One who rapha, heals, promising that obedience keeps His people from the diseases inflicted on Egypt.
basic.typology: The bitter water made sweet by something cast into it echoes throughout Scripture's pattern of God transforming what is unusable into a source of life, later fulfilled when Christ turns bitterness, sin, and death itself into life for those united to Him.
basic.christ: God names Himself here the LORD who heals, a title that anticipates Christ's ministry of healing bodies as a sign of the greater healing He brings to sin-sick souls, and ultimately the full and final healing of all things in the new creation, Revelation 22:2.
basic.god: God is patient with a people who complain almost immediately after praising Him, meeting their grumbling not with abandonment but with provision. Yet He also uses ordinary hardship as a genuine test, wanting obedience that flows from trust, not mere memory of past deliverance.
basic.crossReferences: James 1:2-4 speaks of trials testing faith to produce endurance, echoing the testing at Marah. Revelation 22:1-2 pictures water and healing finally perfected in the new creation. Deuteronomy 8:2-3 recalls this wilderness testing as designed to reveal what was in Israel's heart.
basic.oneStory: Even freshly redeemed people grumble quickly when the next hardship comes, and God meets that grumbling not with rejection but with provision and a test of trust. This pattern, God's care meeting human weakness in the wilderness, points toward Christ, who leads His people through every wilderness to a rest and healing this world cannot give.

context.literary:
These six verses are short, but they are built with care and they open a new section of the book. Exodus 15:22 to 18:27 is the journey from the sea to Sinai, and it is made of a chain of crises: bitter water at Marah, hunger in the Desert of Sin, no water at Rephidim, and war with Amalek. Marah is the first link, and it lays down the pattern for the rest. A need arises, the people grumble, Moses cries out, the LORD provides, and a lesson is drawn.

The placement right after the song is deliberate. The song ended with Israel confident that God would guide them 'with loving devotion,' verse 13, and that the nations would be as still as stone before them. Verse 22 begins, 'Then Moses led Israel from the Red Sea,' and within three verses the singers are asking, 'What are we to drink?' The narrator sets praise and complaint side by side without comment and lets the reader feel the drop.

The scene moves in two halves. Verses 22 to 25a are narrative: journey, bitter water, grumbling, prayer, the log, sweet water. Verses 25b to 26 turn to covenant speech, marked by the word 'there' used twice: 'There the LORD made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there He tested them.' The miracle becomes the setting for instruction, and the passage closes on God's self-naming, 'I am the LORD who heals you.'

Verse 27 then acts as a coda. After bitterness comes abundance: twelve springs and seventy palm trees, and the people camp 'by the waters.' Numbers of completeness frame the stop, and the section ends in rest before the next test begins in chapter 16. The reader is shown in miniature the whole wilderness road: testing, grace, and a place of refreshment along the way.
context.historical:
The Desert of Shur lies on the eastern edge of Egypt, in the northwest of the Sinai peninsula. The name appears earlier in Genesis: Hagar fled from Sarah toward Egypt and was found by a spring 'along the road to Shur,' Genesis 16:7, and Ishmael's descendants settled 'from Havilah to Shur, which is near the border of Egypt,' Genesis 25:18. Numbers 33:8 calls the same stretch the Wilderness of Etham, and it confirms the three days' march before the camp at Marah.

The three days carry an edge. From the start Moses had asked Pharaoh for a 'three-day journey into the wilderness' so that Israel could sacrifice to the LORD, Exodus 3:18 and 5:3. Now, three days out, instead of a feast of worship they find a spring they cannot drink. The first real test comes at the very point the journey had been aimed at.

Springs in this region are often brackish, and travellers have long reported bitter or salty wells along the likely route. The text does not explain the means by which the log changed the water, and it does not treat it as a technique. The LORD 'showed' Moses the wood, and the result is credited to Him.

For an Israelite hearer, bitterness had a history. The Egyptians had 'made their lives bitter with hard labor,' Exodus 1:14, and at the Passover Israel ate bitter herbs as a memorial of that slavery, Exodus 12:8. The people have left the bitterness of Egypt only to meet it again in the water. The promise about 'the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians,' verse 26, would also have been vivid to people who had just watched the boils and plagues fall on Egypt.

Elim, with its springs and palms, is usually located further south along the western side of the peninsula. Numbers 33:9 records the same twelve springs and seventy palm trees, a detail the travellers evidently remembered.
context.canonical:
The Marah episode is the first of a series of wilderness complaints that the rest of Scripture keeps returning to. Before Sinai, in Exodus 15 to 17, God meets complaint with provision and no punishment. After Sinai, in Numbers 11 to 21, similar complaints about food and water often bring judgment, because the people now stand under a covenant they have sworn to keep. The contrast begins here, where God first 'made for them a statute and an ordinance.'

Deuteronomy explains why the wilderness tested Israel: 'so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments,' Deuteronomy 8:2. The promise about Egypt's diseases is expanded into the covenant blessings and curses. 'He will not lay upon you any of the terrible diseases you knew in Egypt,' Deuteronomy 7:15, but disobedience would bring 'all the diseases you dreaded in Egypt,' Deuteronomy 28:60.

The title 'the LORD who heals' echoes through Israel's prayers and prophets. 'I wound and I heal,' Deuteronomy 32:39. 'Heal me, O LORD, and I will be healed,' Jeremiah 17:14. 'He who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases,' Psalm 103:3. Hosea calls a wounded nation to return to the God who 'will heal us,' Hosea 6:1.

Two later scenes echo Marah closely. Elisha casts salt into the bad spring at Jericho and says, 'I have healed this water,' 2 Kings 2:21, using the same verb. Ezekiel sees a river flowing from the temple into the Dead Sea so that its waters become fresh, Ezekiel 47:8-9, the verb again speaking of healing. The healed water at Marah becomes a picture of God's final renewal.

In the New Testament Jesus heals 'all the sick' to fulfil Isaiah's word, Matthew 8:16-17, and Peter joins healing to the cross: 'By His stripes you are healed,' 1 Peter 2:24, quoting Isaiah 53:5. Revelation ends with the river of life and the leaves of the tree that are 'for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to learn that the wilderness would be a school, and that its lessons would come through need. The people had seen the LORD defeat Egypt, but they had not yet learned to trust Him when there was nothing to drink. The narrative shows the right and wrong responses side by side. The people grumble against Moses; Moses cries out to the LORD. Both face the same bitter water, but only one turns to God.

He also wanted them to understand the relationship they were entering. The statute and ordinance given at Marah, and the conditional promise of verse 26, prepare for Sinai. God's rescue comes first, and His commands follow as the way to live in the relationship He has created. Obedience is not the price of redemption; it is the shape of life with the Redeemer.

Most of all, Moses wanted Israel to know the LORD by a new name drawn from experience. They had learned He was a warrior at the sea. At Marah they learn He is their healer, the One who can make the undrinkable good and keep His people whole. Each crisis on the road would teach them something more of who He is.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The log cast into the water is a description of what God did once, not a method to copy. Nothing in the passage invites believers to look for special objects or rituals that release healing. The emphasis falls on the LORD who 'showed' Moses what to do and on the prayer that preceded it.

The conditional promise of verse 26 was spoken to Israel as a nation on the way to the covenant soon to be made at Sinai, and its full form appears in Deuteronomy's blessings and curses. It cannot be turned into a guarantee that faithful individuals will never be ill; Scripture elsewhere shows faithful people suffering, and Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus, 2 Timothy 4:20.

What does carry forward is the character of God and the way He trains His people. Hardship after blessing is not a sign that God has abandoned us, and the right answer to it is Moses' answer: crying out to the LORD rather than grumbling against His servants. 1 Corinthians 10:10-11 applies these wilderness stories directly to the church as warnings written for us.

debates.question: How should the promise in verse 26, that obedience prevents the diseases of Egypt, be applied today?

views.label: A covenant promise specific to Israel
views.case: The promise belongs to the national covenant that is about to be made at Sinai, with its blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience, Deuteronomy 7:15 and 28:60. It concerned Israel as a people in the land, not a universal guarantee of physical health for individual believers.

views.label: A principle of wisdom and God's care
views.case: Others see a broader pattern: life ordered by God's word tends toward wholeness, and God remains the healer of His people. They caution, though, that the righteous can suffer, as Job shows, so the principle describes God's character rather than a formula.

views.label: Fulfilled in Christ's healing
views.case: A third reading stresses that the promise finds its deepest fulfilment in Christ, who carried our diseases, Matthew 8:17, and whose wounds heal, 1 Peter 2:24. Its full bodily realisation awaits the resurrection and the new creation, Revelation 21:4.

debates.bearing: All three agree that verse 26 is not a transaction in which obedience buys health. It reveals the LORD as healer, calls His people to listen to Him, and points forward to the complete healing that only the new creation will bring.

debates.question: Is the log that sweetened the water meant to be read as a picture of the cross?

views.label: A historical provision only
views.case: The text says only that the LORD showed Moses a piece of wood and the water became sweet. It draws no symbolic meaning from the wood, and the point is God's power and instruction, not the object. Reading the cross into it risks allegory.

views.label: A picture the church rightly saw
views.case: Many early Christian writers saw the wood cast into bitter water as a picture of the cross, which turns bitterness to sweetness. The Hebrew word for the log is the ordinary word for tree, and the New Testament speaks of Christ hung on a tree, Acts 5:30 and Galatians 3:13.

debates.bearing: The New Testament never cites Marah, so the cross is not the meaning of the text. But the link can be held as a legitimate echo, provided it serves the text's own point: God alone turns what brings death into what gives life.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb for 'grumbled' in verse 24 is lun, and it is one of the signature words of the wilderness stories. It appears here, then repeatedly in Exodus 16 and in Exodus 17:3, and again in Numbers 14 to 17. It describes more than a complaint: it is a muttering resentment directed at leaders, and Moses will soon insist that it is really aimed at God, Exodus 16:8. Marah is where the word first enters the story.

The LORD 'showed' Moses a log. The verb is yarah in its causative form, which means to point out, direct or teach. It is the root from which the noun torah, 'instruction' or 'law,' comes. The choice of verb suits the scene. Before God gives Israel any statutes, He teaches Moses how to make bitter water sweet, and in the very next sentence He gives them 'a statute and an ordinance.'

The word for 'log' is ets, the ordinary Hebrew word for tree or wood. It is the word used of the trees of the garden in Genesis 2:9 and of the tree of life. The Greek Old Testament rendered it with xylon, wood or tree, the word the New Testament uses when it speaks of Christ hung 'on a tree,' Acts 5:30 and 1 Peter 2:24.

The pair 'statute and ordinance,' choq umishpat, describes binding decrees and just rulings. The same pair appears when Joshua renews the covenant at Shechem, 'there at Shechem he established for them a statute and ordinance,' Joshua 24:25. Marah is a small foretaste of covenant making, before Sinai.

God 'tested' Israel, from nasah. The verb describes proving someone to show what is in them. It is used when God tested Abraham, Genesis 22:1, and when Moses explains Sinai's terrors, 'God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you,' Exodus 20:20. The same root will name Massah, 'testing,' in Exodus 17:7, where the roles are reversed and Israel tests God.

Verse 26 piles up four conditions, and the first uses an emphatic Hebrew doubling, literally 'if listening you will listen,' which the BSB renders 'listen carefully.' The verbs of the verse, listen, do, give ear, keep, anticipate the vocabulary of Deuteronomy.

The title 'the LORD who heals you' uses a participle of rapha, so it describes an ongoing identity rather than a single act: He is your healer. The verb covers physical healing, the restoration of land and water, 2 Kings 2:21, and the healing of a nation's sin and backsliding, Hosea 6:1 and Jeremiah 3:22. Finally, Marah is from the root marar, 'to be bitter,' the same root as the bitter herbs of the Passover and the bitterness of slavery in Exodus 1:14, and Naomi takes it as her name, 'Call me Mara,' Ruth 1:20.

typology.type: The wood cast into bitter water, Exodus 15:25
typology.fulfillment: The water could not be drunk until God showed Moses a piece of wood and it was cast in. The New Testament does not cite Marah, but it does speak of the tree on which Christ bore the curse, Galatians 3:13, and bore our sins, 1 Peter 2:24. Through that tree the bitterness of sin and death is turned into life for those who believe. The correspondence is an echo rather than a declared type, and it falls short: the log changed one spring for a moment, while the cross reconciles 'all things,' Colossians 1:20.

God names Himself Israel's healer, protecting them from Egypt's diseases. Jesus heals all who come to Him, and Matthew says He did so 'to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases,' Matthew 8:17. The escalation is that Christ heals not only bodies but the deeper sickness of sin, 'I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners,' Mark 2:17. His healings were signs pointing forward to the resurrection body and the world where there is no more pain, Revelation 21:4.

Israel was tested at Marah and failed, grumbling instead of trusting. Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tested and answered each temptation with Deuteronomy's words about the wilderness years, Matthew 4:1-10. He is the faithful Son who passes the test Israel failed. The type is surpassed in that His obedience is counted for His people, and He is now 'able to help those who are being tempted,' Hebrews 2:18.

After bitterness God brought His people to twelve springs and seventy palm trees and let them rest by the waters. Psalm 23:2 speaks of the shepherd who leads His flock 'beside quiet waters,' and Revelation 7:17 promises that the Lamb 'will lead them to springs of living water.' The Elim rest was a single stop on the way, and the journey resumed; the final springs are the end of the journey, where God 'will wipe away every tear.'

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first by the name God gives Himself. 'I am the LORD who heals you' is spoken to a people who had just seen what God could do to Egypt's bodies and waters, and it promised that He would use the same power for their good. In the Gospels, healing is one of the clearest marks of who Jesus is. When John the Baptist asks whether He is the one to come, Jesus answers by pointing to the blind who see and the lame who walk, Matthew 11:4-5. Matthew reads His healing ministry as fulfilling Isaiah's promise, 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases,' Matthew 8:17. The LORD who heals has come in person.

It leads to Christ by the deeper sickness it exposes. The real problem at Marah was not the water but the people's hearts; three days after singing, they were already grumbling. Jesus said, 'It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick,' Mark 2:17, and He came for sinners. Isaiah had said that the Servant would be 'pierced for our transgressions' and that 'by His stripes we are healed,' Isaiah 53:5, and Peter applies it to the cross, 1 Peter 2:24. The healer is also the one wounded for the healing.

It leads to Christ by pattern, since He relived Israel's wilderness faithfully. Israel was tested and grumbled; Jesus was tested for forty days and trusted His Father, Matthew 4:1-4. Israel asked, 'What are we to drink?'; Jesus, thirsting on the cross, John 19:28, drank the bitter cup His Father gave Him, John 18:11.

There is also a picture, carefully held. The piece of wood cast into bitter water was taken by many early Christians as a picture of the cross, which turns the bitterness of death into life. The New Testament does not draw that line itself, so it should not be pressed as the meaning of the text. But it fits what the New Testament does say: that Christ 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24, and through that tree the curse is lifted, Galatians 3:13.

Finally, the passage points to Christ by its end. After Marah comes Elim, abundant springs and rest. Jesus offers the water that becomes 'a fount of water springing up to eternal life,' John 4:14, and in the new creation the Lamb leads His people to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17, where the tree of life gives leaves 'for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who leads His people into hardship on purpose. Moses 'led Israel from the Red Sea,' verse 22, but Moses was following the cloud, Exodus 13:21. The three dry days and the bitter spring were on the road God chose. That is uncomfortable, but it is honest: God's guidance does not avoid difficulty, and He uses difficulty to test and train, verse 25.

He answers prayer directly. Moses 'cried out to the LORD,' and the LORD responded at once, not with a lecture but with a solution. The grumbling of the people is not answered with rebuke here. Before Sinai, God's patience is striking; He provides first and teaches after.

He is a God who teaches. The verb 'showed' belongs to the family of the word torah. God does not simply fix the water; He instructs Moses, and He then gives the people statutes and ordinances. His provision and His instruction come together. He wants a people who not only receive His gifts but listen to His voice, verse 26.

He reveals Himself by name through experience. 'I am the LORD who heals you' is the first time God calls Himself healer. His names in Scripture are never abstract; each is tied to something He has done or promised. Healing belongs to His character; sickness and the diseases of Egypt are within His power, and He can withhold them or remove them.

The passage also holds together His sovereignty and His covenant faithfulness. Verse 26 says the diseases of Egypt were ones 'I inflicted.' The same God who judged Egypt heals Israel. There is no second power behind the plagues. Deuteronomy 32:39 puts it plainly: 'I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal.' That can be hard to hear, but it means that nothing His people suffer is outside His hand.

Finally, He is generous beyond the need. At Marah the people needed drinkable water; at Elim He gave twelve springs and shade of seventy palms. God's provision is not grudging.

For worship, this passage invites us to bring our bitter places to God in prayer rather than grumbling against others, to listen to His word as the path of life, and to know Him as the healer whose final healing is still ahead.

crossReferences.note: Moses was told to ask Pharaoh for a three-day journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to the LORD. The three days to Marah, Exodus 15:22, reach exactly that point, and the first test comes where Israel expected to worship. The contrast sharpens the disappointment and shows the purpose of the journey is being tested.

The Egyptians 'made their lives bitter with hard labor,' using the same root as Marah. Israel has escaped the bitterness of slavery only to meet bitterness in the water. The echo invites the reader to see the choice before them: to trust God in hardship or to look back to Egypt.

The itinerary of the journey confirms the three days in the Wilderness of Etham, the camp at Marah, and the twelve springs and seventy palm trees at Elim. It shows that the Marah and Elim stops were remembered as fixed points on Israel's route.

Moses explains the purpose of the wilderness years: God led them to humble them and test them, 'to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments.' The testing announced at Marah, Exodus 15:25, is the first instance of this purpose.

Expands the promise of Exodus 15:26: 'He will not lay upon you any of the terrible diseases you knew in Egypt.' The Marah promise becomes part of the covenant blessings, while Deuteronomy 28:60 warns that disobedience will bring those diseases back.

Elisha casts salt into the bad spring at Jericho and announces, 'I have healed this water.' Like Marah, a simple object is cast in and the water is made good, and the verb of healing links it to the LORD who heals. The power belongs to God's word, not the object.

A river flows from the temple into the Dead Sea and makes its waters fresh, so that life swarms wherever it goes. The healing of bitter water at Marah grows into a vision of God healing the most lifeless waters of the land from His dwelling place.

David blesses the LORD 'who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases.' The psalm joins the name revealed at Marah with the forgiveness of sin, showing that God's healing reaches the soul as well as the body.

Jesus drives out spirits with a word and heals all the sick, fulfilling Isaiah's words, 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases.' The LORD who heals at Marah is present in person, and He heals by carrying what He removes.

Paul warns the church not to complain as the wilderness generation did. These things 'happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us.' The grumbling that begins at Marah, Exodus 15:24, is held up as a mirror for believers.

The river of the water of life flows from the throne, and the leaves of the tree of life are 'for the healing of the nations.' The healed water of Marah and the name 'the LORD who heals' reach their final fulfilment in the city of God.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God gave the first humans a garden watered by a river, Genesis 2:10, with every tree good for food. After the fall, the ground was cursed and life became toil, Genesis 3:17-19. Marah is a small window onto that fallen world: water that should give life but cannot be drunk, a people who have been rescued but whose hearts are still quick to complain. Redemption from Egypt has begun, but the effects of the fall are still everywhere, in the land and in the people.

The passage answers the question the song left open. The song promised that God would lead His redeemed people to His dwelling. Marah shows what that leading will involve: a road through dry places where trust is tested. It also shows God's way on that road. He does not remove His people from the wilderness, but He meets them in it, providing, teaching and healing.

What Marah sets up is the whole pattern of Israel's life with God. The statute and ordinance given here point ahead to Sinai. The testing points ahead to forty years in the wilderness, and to the question Deuteronomy asks: what is in Israel's heart? The promise about Egypt's diseases points ahead to the covenant blessings and curses. And Israel's history will show that the people's deepest sickness was the one Marah first exposed, a heart that forgets and grumbles.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, who took Israel's wilderness road and trusted where Israel grumbled, and who heals by being wounded, Isaiah 53:5. The church now lives in the wilderness between redemption and arrival, with real hardships and real provision, warned by Israel's example and sustained by the same healer.

The story ends with the healing Marah pictured. In the new creation a river flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, clear as crystal, and the tree of life stands beside it, its leaves for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:1-2. There is no more curse, Revelation 22:3, and no more bitter water. The LORD who heals will have healed completely.

quiz.q: How long had Israel gone without finding water before reaching Marah?

options.text: Three days.
options.note: Verse 22 states this precisely, only three days after the Red Sea crossing.

options.text: Forty days.
options.note: Forty is a significant later wilderness number, but not the figure given here; it is three days.

options.text: A full year.
options.note: The text specifies three days, a very short span after their great deliverance.

options.text: The text gives no length of time.
options.note: Verse 22 explicitly states three days.

quiz.q: How did the LORD make the bitter water drinkable?

options.text: He showed Moses a log, which Moses cast into the water, and it was sweetened.
options.note: Verse 25 describes this exact means of provision.

options.text: He commanded the people to boil the water first.
options.note: The text specifies the log cast into the water, not a boiling process.

options.text: He led them to a different water source entirely, bypassing Marah.
options.note: The text says the water at Marah itself was made sweet, not that they avoided it.

options.text: The water became drinkable on its own without any divine action.
options.note: The text credits the LORD directly with showing Moses the means of provision.

quiz.q: What did the people do when they first found the water at Marah bitter?

options.text: They grumbled against Moses, asking what they were to drink.
options.note: Verse 24 records their complaint directly.

options.text: They immediately trusted God to provide without complaint.
options.note: The text explicitly records grumbling, not calm trust, as their first response.

options.text: They returned to Egypt on their own.
options.note: There is no return to Egypt in this passage; they grumble, but stay and see God's provision.

options.text: They attacked Moses physically.
options.note: The text describes verbal grumbling, not a physical attack.

quiz.q: What title does the LORD give Himself in verse 26?

options.text: The LORD who heals you.
options.note: This is the exact title given, tied to Israel's obedience and God's covenant care.

options.text: The LORD who provides.
options.note: That title, Yahweh Yireh, comes from Genesis 22:14, a different passage, not this one.

options.text: The LORD our righteousness.
options.note: That title appears in Jeremiah 23:6, not in this passage.

options.text: No title is given in this passage.
options.note: Verse 26 explicitly gives the title, the LORD who heals you.

quiz.q: What did Israel find when they arrived at Elim?

options.text: Twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees.
options.note: Verse 27 gives these exact numbers, a place of rest and abundance.

options.text: A dry desert with no water at all.
options.note: Elim is described as a place of abundant water and shade, the opposite of a dry desert.

options.text: A hostile army waiting to attack them.
options.note: No army or conflict is mentioned at Elim; it is a place of rest.

options.text: Nothing of note; the text gives no description.
options.note: Verse 27 gives a specific, vivid description of abundance at Elim.

questions: Israel grumbled just three days after singing God's praises at the sea. How quickly does your own gratitude fade when the next hardship comes, even after clear evidence of God's care?

God did not rebuke Israel's need for water; He met it, even while testing their hearts in the process. Where might God be provided for you in a real need while also using the situation to test and grow your trust?
God revealed a new name of Himself, the LORD who heals, exactly at the point of Israel's helplessness. What part of your life right now most needs to know God specifically as healer?
After the bitterness of Marah came the abundance of Elim, twelve springs and seventy palm trees. Can you look back and see a similarly generous provision that followed a hard season in your own life?
The testing at Marah was meant to reveal what was really in Israel's heart. What does your typical response to minor inconveniences reveal about the depth of your trust in God?

translationNotes.note: Marah is the Hebrew word for bitter; the place name functions as a direct commentary on both the water and, implicitly, the people's complaint.
Statute and ordinance likely refers to a general principle of covenant obedience established here, prior to the fuller law given later at Sinai, rather than a specific detailed regulation.
I am the LORD who heals you renders the Hebrew Yahweh Rapha, a covenant name that became foundational to later Israelite and Christian confession of God's character as healer.
